EE301 — Electromagnetic Waves

Transmission lines, from zero. Part I is built from your lecture notes (22 pages), with every derivation filled in. Part II adds the textbook material your lectures skipped.

READ THIS FIRSTThe whole course in six sentences

If you remember nothing else
  1. A wire stops being a wire and becomes a transmission line when it is long compared to a wavelength. Then voltage depends on where you are, not just when.
  2. Modelling the line as infinitely many tiny – sections gives the telegrapher's equations, which combine into the 1-D wave equation. Signals travel at .
  3. For a wave going one way, the line forces a fixed ratio : the characteristic impedance.
  4. A load cannot satisfy that ratio, so a reflected wave is born: . This single formula is 50% of the course.
  5. Forward + reflected waves interfere ⇒ standing waves, maxima and minima every , measured by VSWR.
  6. Looking into the line from distance , you see a transformed impedance . A line inverts normalised impedance; a line repeats it. That is where all the tricks come from.

Not sure what “the wave” even refers to? Start at Ground Floor below — it builds the picture from ordinary circuit theory, with diagrams, before any formula appears.

Everything below expands those six points. Boxes marked INTUITION are for understanding, DERIVATION for the algebra you may be asked to reproduce, EXAM for what actually gets asked.

GROUND FLOOR — START HEREWhat "the wave" actually is

If the word "wave" in this course feels like it arrived from nowhere, that is because it did. Nobody tells you the one thing that has to change in your head first. Here it is, slowly.

Step 1 — what you currently believe about a wire

In every circuits course you have taken, a wire has one voltage. Touch a probe anywhere along it and you read the same number. If the battery says 5 V, the whole wire is at 5 V — instantly, everywhere.

This is a very good approximation. It is also, strictly speaking, false.

Step 2 — the one physical fact that breaks it

Electricity is not instant. When you close a switch, the "news" that the voltage has changed travels down the wire at a finite speed — typically around m/s, about two-thirds the speed of light. Fast, but not infinite.

So picture a long wire and a switch closing at . Take a photograph of the whole wire at three different moments:

This is the whole idea

Look at the middle row. At that single instant, the left half of the wire is at 5 V and the right half is at 0 V.

Two points on one continuous piece of copper, at the same moment, holding different voltages. Circuit theory says that cannot happen. It happens.

The moment voltage depends on where you are as well as when, you are no longer doing circuit theory. You are doing wave theory. That is the entire reason this course exists.

Step 3 — now wiggle the source instead of switching it once

A step gives you one travelling edge. Now suppose the source is a sine generator, oscillating up and down forever. It keeps launching new "news" down the wire, continuously.

The result is that the voltage-versus-position picture stops being a single step and becomes a repeating ripple, sliding along the wire. That ripple is "the wave."

Step 4 — the graph you have never drawn before

Here is where most of the confusion lives. There are two completely different graphs you can draw, and they look identical, and they mean opposite things.

Read the difference carefully

Graph A ( against ). Pick one point on the wire. Stand there. Watch the voltage go up and down as time passes. This is what an oscilloscope shows you, and it is the only graph you have ever drawn. The repeat distance is a period , measured in seconds.

Graph B ( against ). Freeze time. Photograph the entire wire at one instant. Plot the voltage you find at every position. The repeat distance is a wavelength , measured in metres.

When this course says "the wave," it means Graph B — a shape laid out in space, along the wire. Everything that follows — wavelength, standing waves, "a quarter-wave line" — is about that spatial shape. If you keep picturing Graph A, none of it will make sense, because none of it is about time.

The two are linked by the speed: in one period the pattern slides forward by exactly one wavelength, so .

Step 5 — so when does any of this matter?

You now have two lengths in metres that you can compare directly:

  • — the distance over which the voltage pattern completes one full wiggle.
  • — the length of your actual wire.

Lay the wire against the wave and look:

The punchline

If your wire is short compared to , it only ever sits on a tiny, nearly flat piece of the wave. Both ends read the same voltage. Circuit theory is fine. We call this lumped.

If your wire is comparable to or longer, a whole wiggle fits on it. One end can be at  V while a point halfway along is at  V. We call this distributed, and everything in Sections 1–19 follows.

The number that measures "short or long compared to " is the ratio — and dressed up in radians, that is exactly the you meet in the next section. Nothing more.

The two habits to break
  1. "A wire has one voltage." It does not. It has a voltage profile — a different number at every point.
  2. "A wave means something moving up and down in time." Here it means a shape spread out along the wire. Time makes that shape slide; it is not what makes it a wave.

SECTION 0Why any of this exists

In circuit theory you were told a wire is a wire: the same voltage appears at both ends, instantly. That is a lie that stops working at high frequency.

A lumped circuit assumes a signal change propagates across the whole circuit instantaneously. Your resistor "knows" immediately what the source did. That is fine when the physical size of the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength of the signal.

A distributed circuit (a transmission line) is one where that assumption fails: the signal takes real time to travel, so and are functions of both position and time — written , .

The criterion

Signals travel at speed . In one period a wave covers one wavelength, . The question is how that wavelength compares to the length of your line, . The number that measures it is called the electrical length:

Where does come from?

It is a unit conversion, not a physical law. Build it in two steps.

Step 1 — what is. is a rate: the number of radians of phase the wave picks up per metre travelled. Units: rad/m.

Step 2 — pin the rate down. By definition, one wavelength is one complete cycle of the wave, and one complete cycle is radians. So:

Divide both sides by to get radians per metre:

That is the entire derivation. Then is just rate distance — the same structure as :

Intuition — what the number is telling you

Look at the middle of that fraction. The piece is simply how many wavelengths fit onto your line. The only converts that count into radians.

So answers one question: how much of a wave is sitting on the line at any instant?

  • → rad. Both ends of the line are at essentially the same point in the wave's cycle, so the voltage is the same everywhere. Ordinary circuit theory works.
  • → . A whole wave fits on the line: one end can be at a peak while the other sits at a trough. Circuit theory is dead.

The single sentence worth memorising:

is the phase difference, in radians, between the two ends of the line.

This is also why it is called electrical length. The length in metres means nothing by itself — only the length relative to the wavelength matters. The same 10 cm wire is electrically invisible at 1 kHz and electrically enormous at 1 GHz, and is the one number that tells the two situations apart.

Worked check — the same wire at two frequencies

Take m/s and a cm m trace.

At GHz:

Exactly one wavelength sits on the line. Firmly distributed.

At kHz:

Utterly negligible. Lumped. Same piece of copper, opposite conclusions.

Hence the rule:

  •  () → delay is negligible → treat as lumped.
  • or bigger → must use transmission line theory.

Your notes make this concrete with m/s:

FrequencyWavelength Does a 10 cm PCB trace matter?

1 GHz10 cmYes. . Full wave behaviour.
Intuition

It is not "high frequency" that matters — it is length measured in wavelengths. A 1 kHz signal on a 200 km undersea cable is absolutely a transmission line problem. A 1 GHz signal across a 1 mm chip is not. This is why the theory was invented for telegraph cables (hence "telegrapher's equations") long before radio.

THE TOOLKIT — BUILD THIS FIRSTThe five things the rest of the course assumes

From here on, every page uses five ideas without stopping to explain them: inductance, capacitance, KVL/KCL, phasors, and impedance. If any of those are shaky, the maths later will look like magic. So here they are, slowly, from the bottom.

How to use this section

T1, T2, T3 you need before Section 1. T4 and T5 you only need from Section 7 onward — you can skip them on a first pass and come back.

T1 — Inductance: why a plain wire fights you

Start with a fact from physics: a current creates a magnetic field around it. Not just in a coil — any current, in any wire, at all times. The field wraps around the wire in circles.

That field holds energy. To make the field bigger you must put energy in; when it shrinks, you get energy back. So changing the current is not free — and the circuit experiences that cost as a voltage appearing across the wire.

The relationship turns out to be beautifully simple:

Read that equation in words

The voltage across an inductor does not depend on how much current is flowing. It depends on how fast the current is changing. That is what means: the rate of change of .

Big steady current, not changing? Zero volts. Tiny current that flips direction very fast? Possibly enormous volts.

Why this matters for us

Two consequences you will use constantly:

  • At DC, an inductor is invisible. constant ⇒ ⇒ . It behaves as a plain piece of wire. This is why nobody mentioned inductance in your DC circuits course.
  • At high frequency, it dominates. A sinusoid at frequency changes faster as rises, so grows, so the voltage grows. The higher the frequency, the more the wire fights.

That single asymmetry — harmless at DC, brutal at GHz — is half the reason this entire course exists.

You do not need a coil. A straight wire has inductance simply because current flows through it. For coaxial cable it is roughly 250 nH per metre. We write it as per unit length, units H/m.

T2 — Capacitance: why two wires near each other store charge

Take any two conductors separated by a gap. Push charge onto one; an equal and opposite charge is attracted onto the other. Charge is now stored, and a voltage appears between them.

Getting to the equation

The stored charge is proportional to the voltage: . The constant is the capacitance — how much charge you get per volt.

Current is, by definition, the rate at which charge moves: .

Substitute and differentiate:

The pattern — and the mirror image

Compare the two equations you now have. They are mirror images:

  • Inductor: . Resists change in current. Short circuit at DC.
  • Capacitor: . Resists change in voltage. Open circuit at DC.

Swap and and one becomes the other. This symmetry runs through the whole course — you will meet it again as and .

Again, no component needed: any two wires running alongside each other are a capacitor. Coax is about 100 pF per metre. We write per unit length, units F/m.

Where this is going

A transmission line is two conductors running side by side. So it automatically, unavoidably has both: inductance along it, and capacitance across it. Not because someone added components — because of what it physically is. Section 1 does nothing more than take that seriously.

T3 — KVL and KCL: the only two circuit laws we use

Why they are true

KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law). Voltage is like height on a hill. Walk any closed loop and you must return to the height you started at, so all the rises and drops cancel. Going round a circuit loop, the voltages sum to zero.

KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law). Charge is not created or destroyed and does not pile up at a junction. So the current arriving equals the current leaving.

How we will use them

In Section 1 we chop the line into slices of length and apply exactly these two laws to one slice:

  • KVL across the slice, through the series inductance → tells us how voltage changes with position.
  • KCL at the node, with current leaking into the shunt capacitance → tells us how current changes with position.

Those two statements are the telegrapher's equations. Nothing more sophisticated is involved.

T4 — Phasors: why complex numbers turn up in a circuits course

This is the part that looks like it came from nowhere. It did not. It is a labour-saving trick, and here is the labour it saves.

The problem

Once the source is a sinusoid, every voltage and current in the circuit is of the form . To add two of them, or differentiate them, you need trigonometric identities, and it becomes miserable fast. We want something better.

Step 1: what actually is

— but do not think of it as a "number that does not exist." Think of it as an instruction: rotate by 90°.

Draw numbers as arrows from the origin. The number is an arrow pointing right. Multiply by and it rotates a quarter turn, to point up. Multiply by again and it points left — which is . And indeed . The algebra and the geometry agree.

Step 2: Euler's formula

Do not panic at this. It says one thing: is an arrow of length 1, pointing at angle . Its horizontal shadow is , its vertical shadow is . That is the whole content.

Step 3: let the angle grow with time

Now put . As increases, the angle increases, so is an arrow spinning steadily anticlockwise, at radians per second.

The idea in one line

A sine wave is the shadow of something going round in a circle. So instead of tracking a wiggly curve through time, track the arrow. The arrow has just two numbers — length (the amplitude) and angle (the phase) — and they do not change with time.

Writing it down properly

Take our sinusoid and pull it apart:

The spinning part is the same for everything in the circuit — every voltage and current oscillates at the source frequency. So it carries no useful information, and we simply stop writing it.

What is left, , is the phasor: one complex number holding the amplitude and the phase. To recover the real signal, multiply by and take the real part.

Step 4: the payoff — calculus becomes multiplication

The one line that justifies the entire method

Differentiate the spinning arrow:

Differentiating gave back the same thing, times . So in phasor world:

Why this is such a big deal

Differential equations become ordinary algebra. That is the whole reason for the detour through complex numbers — not elegance, laziness. Every in the telegrapher's equations becomes a , and a partial differential equation collapses into something you can solve with GCSE algebra.

The geometric reason it works: differentiating a cosine gives a negative sine, which is the same wave shifted by 90°. And multiplying by is rotating by 90°. The calculus and the rotation are the same operation.

T5 — Impedance: Ohm's law for things that are not resistors

Now feed each component its phasor and see what comes out as.

Derivation — all three components

Resistor. , no derivatives, nothing changes:

Inductor. . Replace with :

Capacitor. , so :

In every case the ratio is a single (complex) number. We call it the impedance , and now one law covers everything:

What the real and imaginary parts mean physically

Real part — dissipation. Energy goes in and does not come back; it leaves as heat. Only resistance does this.

Imaginary part — storage. Energy is borrowed for part of the cycle and handed back later. Nothing is lost. This is called reactance, written , and .

Sign of the imaginary part: is inductive (voltage leads current), is capacitive (current leads voltage).

Notice both reactances depend on : the inductor's grows with frequency, the capacitor's shrinks. Change the frequency and the whole circuit behaves differently — which is exactly why a wire that is fine at 1 kHz misbehaves at 1 GHz.

Why you should care, specifically

Nearly every result in the rest of this course is a statement about impedance:

  • — the impedance a line demands.
  • — reflections happen when two impedances disagree.
  • — the line transforms one impedance into another.
  • A shorted stub gives — purely imaginary, so purely storage, so a piece of wire has become an inductor or a capacitor.

If "impedance" means something concrete to you, those all read as sentences rather than symbols.

Checklist before Section 1
  1. An inductor's voltage depends on the rate of change of current: .
  2. A capacitor's current depends on the rate of change of voltage: .
  3. Any two conductors side by side have both, per metre, automatically.
  4. KVL: voltages round a loop sum to zero. KCL: current in = current out.
  5. A phasor is a static arrow: length = amplitude, angle = phase. becomes .
  6. Impedance is : real part burns energy, imaginary part stores it.

SECTION 1The distributed model & telegrapher's equations

Take any two parallel conductors (coaxial cable, two metal strips, twisted pair). Two facts of electromagnetism:

  • Current flowing along them creates magnetic flux → there is inductance per unit length (H/m).
  • A voltage difference between them stores charge → there is capacitance per unit length (F/m).

So model a short slice of length as a series inductor and a shunt capacitor , and chain infinitely many of them.

Derivation — the two telegrapher's equations

KVL around one slice. The voltage dropped across the series inductor is :

Divide by and let . The left side is :

KCL at one node. Whatever current does not continue forward must charge the shunt capacitor:

Intuition

Read them in words: (1) voltage falls along the line because current is changing — series inductance resists changes in current. (2) current falls along the line because voltage is changing — some current is being diverted to charge the shunt capacitance.

They are coupled: a change in makes a change in , which makes a change in further along… That chain reaction is the propagating wave. It is exactly the same mathematics as a mass-on-springs chain, or a rope: inertia () trading energy with a restoring element ().

SECTION 3Characteristic impedance

The single most important idea in the course: for a wave travelling one way, the line dictates a fixed ratio between voltage and current.

Derivation — forward wave

Assume a purely forward wave. Voltage and current must have the same shape (both obey the same wave equation and are coupled by (1)):

Substitute into telegrapher's equation (1), :

Cancel (true for all , so the coefficients must match):

Backward wave. Repeat with , so and the LHS flips sign:

Where the minus sign comes from — students lose marks here

It is not that the backward wave has negative impedance. It is a bookkeeping convention: we define positive current as flowing in the direction, for both waves. The backward wave carries power in the direction, so with our fixed sign convention its current comes out negative relative to its voltage. Power then correctly comes out negative (flowing backward).

Hence the total fields on a line are always written:

— note the plus in , minus in . Nearly every derivation in this course starts from these two lines.

Intuition — is not a resistor

An infinitely long line draws current from a source and never gives it back — so it behaves like a resistor of ohms. But no energy is dissipated as heat. The energy is carried away down the line forever. is a property of geometry and materials only (it is , and come from the cross-section) — it does not depend on length, frequency (for a lossless line), or what you connect.

Think of it as the line's "personality": the exchange rate between volts and amps that this particular pipe insists on. 50 Ω and 75 Ω coax are the industry-standard personalities.

Note also and are the two independent combinations of and — between them they contain everything about a lossless line.

Exam

SECTION 4Launching a pulse: the source boundary condition

Generator with internal resistance drives the line at . What actually gets onto the line?

The key insight

At , the source has no idea what is at the far end. Information about the load cannot have reached it yet — that takes (there and back). So for that first instant the line looks like a plain resistor of value , and the circuit is a simple voltage divider.

What each form is for
  • — the direction form. It tells you which way the wave goes and nothing else. Hold the argument constant: means must decrease as increases — motion to the left. ✓
  • The notes' form — the timing form. It additionally pins down when, measured from the moment the source fired. That is what you need for a bounce diagram, where the whole question is what arrives when.

The rule that removes the confusion

A minus sign in the argument of is always a delay, never a direction.

Direction is set by the sign attached to :

Why for a pure reactance

. Numerator and denominator are complex conjugates of each other (up to sign: , and ). Equal magnitudes ⇒ , so : pure phase shift, no loss of amplitude.

Intuition — the rope analogy

Send a pulse down a light rope tied to a wall (a short: the end cannot move). The wall pushes back and the pulse returns upside down — . Tie the rope instead to a frictionless ring on a pole (an open end, free to move). The end overshoots and the pulse returns right way up — . Join the rope to another rope of exactly matched mass per length and nothing comes back at all — .

Impedance mismatch is the electrical version of a rope suddenly changing weight. Reflection is what an interface does when it cannot pass the wave through smoothly.

Passivity constraint

For any physically realisable passive load, , which forces . A reflection cannot come back bigger than it went out. On the complex -plane, all passive loads live inside the unit circle. (That circle is the outline of the Smith chart.)

SECTION 6Multiple reflections and the bounce diagram

The reflected wave travels back to the source. If , it reflects again there, with

and heads back to the load. And again. The pulse rattles back and forth, shrinking each round trip by a factor .

Derivation — the steady-state load voltage

Let be the initially launched wave. Accumulate everything that has arrived at the load as :

Geometric series with ratio (magnitude for passive terminations, so it converges):

Sanity check — it must equal the DC voltage divider. Substitute , :

Exactly the lumped voltage divider. ✓ The line has vanished from the answer.

Where the comes from — and why it is not part of the series

Careful bookkeeping. The waves travelling on the line and the voltage you would measure at the load are not the same thing.

Each time a wave of size arrives at the load, two waves exist there at once: the incident one, and the reflection it immediately creates, . A voltmeter at the load cannot separate them — it reads the sum:

So is the conversion from "size of the wave that arrived" to "voltage actually appearing across the load". It applies once to every arrival, so it factors straight out of the sum:

Two different roles, do not mix them up: converts wave amplitude into measured load voltage. counts up the infinitely many round trips.

Sanity-check it against things you already believe
  • Open circuit (): . The voltage doubles at an open end. The reflected wave arrives in phase and piles on top of the incident one. This is a real effect — it is how an unterminated cable can destroy an input.
  • Short circuit (): . The load voltage is zero — which it must be, because it is a short. The inverted reflection exactly cancels the incident wave.
  • Matched (): . No reflection, so what arrives is what you measure.

If your algebra ever produces a load voltage that does not satisfy these three, you have dropped or double-counted the .

The matching partner for current

Current has the opposite sign, because :

Check: at a short () the current factor is — current doubles, voltage vanishes. At an open () it is — no current, voltage doubles. Exactly swapped, as it should be.

Intuition

This is the punchline of the whole time-domain story: the transmission line only matters during the transient. Once the reflections have died out, the circuit settles into the boring answer you would have got from first-year circuit theory. The line's whole job is the first few nanoseconds — which is precisely when digital signal integrity lives or dies.

Worked example 1 — the staircase

A 9 V step is applied at to a generator of internal resistance , driving a lossless line of whose one-way delay is . The line is terminated in . Sketch and .

Step 2 — the two reflection coefficients.

Both positive, so nothing will invert; the answer will climb monotonically. The round-trip shrink factor is .

Step 3 — the lattice. Each diagonal is the pulse in flight; each bounce multiplies its amplitude by the reflection coefficient at that end.

Why the source end starts at 3 V and the load sits at zero

For the first seconds the load has no idea anything has happened — the news has not arrived, so exactly. Meanwhile the source has been sitting at V since , because from its point of view it is driving a resistor.

The source stays at 3 V until , which is when its own launched wave returns. That delay is the round trip, and it is the single most useful number in the whole problem: it is how long the generator remains ignorant of what it is connected to.

Worked example 2 — when it rings instead

Same idea, but now a low-impedance driver into an unterminated line: V, , , load open-circuit. This is the everyday digital-electronics case.

The load voltage hits 4 V on a 3 V signal — a 33% overshoot — before settling. Every error is of the previous one, so the sign alternates and the magnitude decays.

Reading the sign of before you compute anything
  • — monotonic staircase, approaches the final value from one side, never overshoots. (Example 1.)
  • — damped ringing, alternating overshoot and undershoot. (Example 2.)
  • — one step and done. This is the case the box above calls out.

Stating which of the three you are in, before any arithmetic, is worth a mark on its own and tells you immediately whether your sketch is plausible.

The clean special case:

Redo Example 1 with instead of 100. Then and the whole series collapses:

The wave reflected from the load returns to the source and is completely absorbed, because the source impedance matches the line. Nothing is sent back out, so there is no third, fifth or seventh arrival. Steady state is reached at — one step at the load, one at the source, done.

This is called source termination (or series termination) and it is how real digital drivers are built: you cannot control what the far end looks like, but you can make sure that whatever comes back dies at the driver. Examiners like it because the sketch is two clean steps instead of an infinite staircase.

Four ways this question goes wrong
  1. Forgetting . The lattice carries wave amplitudes; a meter reads the sum of the arriving wave and the one it creates. Plot the wave amplitude by mistake and Example 1 gives 3 V at instead of 4.8 V.
  2. Using in the initial divider. At the load does not exist as far as the source is concerned. It is always , never — that is the answer, not the one.
  3. Putting the load steps at even multiples of . The load is one transit away, so it steps at ; the source steps at They interleave and never coincide.
  4. Not checking convergence. If your staircase does not head for , something is wrong — and finding that out at the end costs nothing.

SECTION 7Sinusoidal steady state: phasors

Sections 4–6 followed a single pulse bouncing around. That works for a pulse. For a source that oscillates forever, waves are arriving and reflecting continuously and forever — tracking them one at a time is hopeless. Phasors solve the whole steady state in one shot.

Before you start

This section leans entirely on T4 in the Toolkit (spinning arrows, , and why becomes ). If that is hazy, read T4 first — the rest of this will be mechanical afterwards.

Step 1 — the observation that makes it all work

Drive a linear circuit with and something remarkable happens: every voltage and every current everywhere in it is also a cosine, at exactly the same frequency . Nothing can create a new frequency — only resistors, inductors and capacitors are present, and none of them can.

So at any point on the line, the voltage looks like

Read carefully what does and does not depend on position:

  • — the same everywhere. Carries no information about .
  • , the amplitude — varies with position.
  • , the phase — varies with position.
The insight

Only two numbers actually change as you move along the line: amplitude and phase. Everything else is fixed. So why drag the whole around in every equation? Track the two numbers that matter and throw away the rest.

Step 2 — pack those two numbers into one complex number

A complex number is a pair (length, angle). Perfect fit. Define

and to get the real signal back, multiply by the spinning part and take the horizontal shadow:

  • — the spinner. Multiplying by it makes the arrow rotate at rad/s.
  • — "take the horizontal shadow." As the arrow spins, its shadow slides back and forth as a cosine.

Now the trick

Every quantity in the circuit carries the same . It appears on both sides of every equation, so it can be cancelled from all of them. We simply stop writing it. From here on we work only with the stationary arrows and .

Nothing is lost. Whenever you want the real waveform back, reattach and take the real part.

The same idea without algebra

If , you conclude . You have not abolished the number 5; it was on both sides, so it told you nothing. is the 5.

Physically: every voltage and current in the circuit is whirling round at the same rate . Imagine stepping onto a carousel spinning at exactly that rate. Ride along, and none of the arrows appear to move at all — but the angles between them, which is the only thing that carries information, are completely unchanged.

The phasor domain is that rotating frame. Time still exists; you have just stopped describing the part of it that is common to everything.

So where is time kept?

In the recipe for getting it back. It was never lost:

Solve the -only equations, then reattach and take the real part whenever you want an actual waveform. Section 8 does exactly this to get the standing-wave patterns.

When you are NOT allowed to do this

The cancellation only works because every quantity shares one common . That requires two conditions:

  1. Linearity. Only , , — no diodes, nothing that could generate new frequencies. A second frequency would have a different exponential and nothing would cancel.
  2. Steady state. Transients must have died away. During the switch-on transient the waveform is not a pure sinusoid, so it cannot be written as a single phasor. That is precisely why Sections 4–6 had to be done in the time domain.

This is why the section is called sinusoidal steady state. The name is a statement of the two assumptions.

SECTION 8Standing waves

A reflection means two waves now exist on the line at once, running in opposite directions. This section works out what their sum looks like — and the answer is strange enough that it gets its own name.

Step 1 — when two waves overlap, you just add them

Transmission lines are linear, so there is no interaction, no collision, no interference in the everyday sense. At each point the total voltage is simply the sum of whatever waves happen to be there:

That is the entire physics of this section. Everything below is just doing that sum carefully for one particular case.

Step 2 — the case to do first: a total reflection

Take an open-circuited line, so and the reflected wave is exactly as big as the incident one, . Write both waves out in the time domain:

(The sign inside the bracket is what sets the direction — see Section 2 if that is not automatic yet.)

Step 3 — do the sum

The algebra, with the identity spelled out

There is a standard trig identity for adding two cosines:

Here and . Work out the two brackets separately:

Substitute back, and use :

Step 4 — read what that result is telling you

Look at the shape of the answer, not the symbols

Compare the two forms side by side:

  • Travelling wave: .   and are locked together inside one bracket. Increase and you can undo it by increasing — which is exactly what "the shape slides along" means.
  • Our answer: .   and have separated into two independent factors. Nothing can slide.

That separation is the mathematical fingerprint of a standing wave. The factor fixes a shape in space, permanently. The factor just scales that whole shape up and down over time — like a rope being shaken, not like a wave rolling along it.

Watch it rather than read it

Standing waves are a motion phenomenon, so still pictures fight you. Press each of the four buttons below and watch what changes. Start with Matched to see what a normal travelling wave looks like, then go to Open and watch the motion stop dead.

Live standing-wave simulator — press a termination and watch
What to look for, in this order
  1. Matched (). One wave, marching steadily right. This is the normal case and the thing to compare everything else against.
  2. Open (). The bold curve stops travelling entirely. Fix your eye on a green dot: the curve is pinned to zero there permanently. Between the dots it just breathes up and down.
  3. Short (). Identical behaviour, but every node has shifted by . Same physics, different starting phase.
  4. Partial (). The honest general case, and the one exams use. It both drifts right and ripples in place. The dips no longer reach zero — and that non-zero minimum is exactly what VSWR measures in Section 9.

Turn off "the two waves" to see only what physically exists on the line. Turn it back on to see why.

If you prefer still frames, here is the same thing frozen at four instants through half a cycle:

The thing to actually notice

Follow one green dotted line down the four frames. At that position, the blue and red curves are always equal and opposite, so their sum is zero — at every instant, forever. It is not that the wave passes through zero there; it is that it is permanently pinned there.

Look at the third frame (): the entire line is momentarily flat. All the energy is in the current at that instant, none in the voltage. A quarter cycle later it will all be back in the voltage. The energy sloshes between the two rather than going anywhere.

Step 5 — where the nodes and antinodes are

Locating them

Nodes (permanently zero) occur wherever the spatial factor vanishes:

Antinodes (maximum swing) occur where it is :

Using to convert each time. The spacings that follow are worth memorising:

  • node to next node:

  • node to the neighbouring antinode:
Worth untangling — "period " vs. "repeats every "

These sound like they contradict each other, but they're answers to two different questions.

The raw signed snapshot , taken literally as a function of , needs a full to return to the exact same signed value everywhere: . That's the "" from the Ground Floor section, where a single travelling wave's photograph repeats every wavelength.

The standing-wave pattern — where the nodes and antinodes physically sit — is a different question, and it repeats every . Move by and : the sign flips, but the zero-crossings don't move and the size of the swing, , is identical. A diode probe sliding along the line reads , not the sign — so every measurable quantity (node positions, VSWR, , ) is blind to that sign flip and repeats every .

Rule of thumb: anything built from a single travelling wave has period . Anything built from the interference between a forward and a backward wave — which is everything from here through Section 16 — carries a factor of or (round-trip phase), and already, so it repeats twice as often, every .

Step 6 — the current does the opposite

Why sines appear instead of cosines

Voltage added because . But current has a minus sign (Section 3), so the two cosines subtract:

The companion identity is , and with the same two brackets as before:

The consequence — and it is a physical one

is zero exactly where peaks. So current nodes sit at voltage antinodes and vice versa, offset by all the way along.

Sanity check at the open end itself: an open circuit forces the current to zero there, and indeed at . Meanwhile , so the voltage is at a maximum. Exactly what an open circuit should do. ✓

Step 7 — why no power flows

Two separate reasons, both worth having

From the algebra: voltage goes as , current as . They are 90° out of phase in time, so the average of over a cycle is zero. No net power.

From common sense: the reflected wave is carrying away exactly as much power as the incident wave delivers, because nothing absorbs anything at an open circuit. Net transfer is zero by bookkeeping.

So a fully reflecting line is not a transmission system at all — it is a resonator. Energy shuttles between the electric field (piled up at voltage antinodes) and the magnetic field (at current antinodes) and never reaches the far end. Section 15 puts this to work deliberately.

Step 8 — the short-circuit case

For a short, , so and the two waves subtract instead. Running the identical algebra swaps the sines and cosines:

Same picture, nodes and antinodes swapped. Which is right: a short forces at , and . ✓

Exam

Given a termination, you should be able to say immediately where the first voltage node sits. Short → node at the load. Open → antinode at the load, first node back. Then everything repeats every . Sketching this correctly usually earns the marks even before any algebra.

SECTION 10: the rotating phasor

This section is the hidden spine of the whole subject. Understand it and Sections 11–12 become obvious.

Define the reflection coefficient at any point, not just at the load: the ratio of backward to forward wave, evaluated there. At :

Derivation

Two consequences, both enormous:

Consequence 1 — the magnitude never changes

Why physically: on a lossless line, power is dissipated only at the load. So the forward power and the backward power are each individually constant along the line, and their ratio must be constant. Only the phase relationship changes with position.

Consequence 2 — everything repeats every

Moving toward the generator by rotates clockwise by angle . A full rotation needs

So , , the standing-wave pattern — everything is periodic in . And a move is a half-turn (), which is why quarter-wave lines invert things.

Intuition — same physics, different language

Section 6's bounce diagram told this exact story in the time domain: a pulse leaves the load, travels back, reflects at the source, comes back again… Section 10 is the sinusoidal version of that. A continuous sine wave doesn't make one round trip and die out — it is always, at every instant, partway through a round trip at every point on the line simultaneously. is "the reflection coefficient, delayed by the round-trip phase " — the exact frequency-domain counterpart of "the reflected pulse, delayed by the round-trip time " from Section 6. Swap a time delay for a space delay and you are translating between the two pictures.

Intuition — this is the Smith chart

Those circle diagrams in your notes with "moving towards generator" arrows are the -plane. The Smith chart is nothing more than this same disc with the curves of constant and constant printed on it, so you can read impedance off a rotation. If you internalise " rotates clockwise, radius fixed, full turn per ", the Smith chart is just a lookup table.

Also note where the load sits tells you the standing-wave picture instantly: whenever the rotating crosses the positive real axis you are at a voltage maximum (and is real and maximal); crossing the negative real axis is a voltage minimum ( real and minimal).

SECTION 12Open, short, and stubs

Set or in form (B). These "stubs" are the workhorses of microwave circuits.

First: what is a stub?

Start here if the word "stub" means nothing to you

A stub is a dead-end piece of cable. That is the whole definition. You take the same transmission line you are already using, cut a length of it, connect one end to your circuit, and then do one of two things to the far end:

  • Short it — solder the inner conductor to the outer. That is a shorted stub.
  • Leave it — just let the end dangle. That is an open stub.

Nothing is connected to the far end. No signal goes anywhere. It is a spur off the side of your circuit that leads nowhere — hence "stub", as in a stub of a branch.

Why a dead end is not useless

The natural objection: if nothing is connected at the far end, how can it do anything?

Because of the one idea this whole course is built on. A wave travels down the stub, hits the end, reflects, and comes back. What you see at the junction is the sum of what you sent in and what returned — and what returned has been delayed by the round trip .

Change the length and you change that delay, which changes how the returning wave lines up against the outgoing one. Sometimes they add, sometimes they cancel, usually something in between. The stub is a component whose value you set by choosing a length.

That is exactly what Section 11 already told you — a line transforms whatever sits at its far end into something else at its input, . A stub is just that formula with the simplest possible : zero, or infinity.

Why anyone bothers

At 1 kHz you would use an inductor. At 5 GHz a real inductor is a disaster: its own self-capacitance resonates, its leads are a significant fraction of a wavelength, and its value is nowhere near what the label says.

But a piece of copper of a precisely known length is trivial to make, and on a printed circuit board it costs nothing — it is just a track. So at microwave frequencies you stop buying components and start cutting lengths of line. That is what the rest of this section is about, and it is the single biggest practical difference between low-frequency and high-frequency circuit design.

The case worth understanding completely: a shorted stub

This one result — a short, viewed a quarter wavelength away, looks like an open — sounds like nonsense the first time you meet it. Here it is three ways.

The confusion to clear up first

Nothing about the short circuit changes. Put a probe on the shorted end and you will measure zero volts, always. The solder joint is still a solder joint.

What changes is where you are standing when you ask the question. "Impedance" is a local ratio at the point you measure. On a line carrying a standing wave, and vary with position in opposite ways — so the ratio is a different number at every point. That is the entire content of Section 11, and the stub is its most dramatic example.

Way 1 — read it off the standing wave

A short forces at its own position, so from Section 8 the pattern on the stub is

with measured from the short. Now evaluate at the two ends:

Position
(the short)maximum — a short ✓
()maximum — an open

Maximum voltage with zero current is an open circuit. Nothing mysterious happened: you simply walked from a voltage node to a voltage antinode, and nodes and antinodes alternate every .

Way 2 — follow the wave round the trip

This is the version that answers "but why does no current flow?"

Push a wave into the stub. It travels to the short, reflects, and travels back — a round trip of , which is of travel phase. At the short it also picks up the reflection phase, , another .

Voltage: (travel) (reflection) . The returning voltage wave arrives back in phase with what you are sending. The two add — large voltage.

Current: here is the asymmetry. Current reflects with the opposite sign to voltage ( at a short), so it gets no from the reflection — only the from travelling. The returning current arrives out of phase and the two cancel — zero current.

Large voltage, zero current, . An open circuit, built out of a short circuit and a delay. ✓

Way 3 — just put the numbers in the formula

and , so . ✓ The formula is the fastest route, but on its own it explains nothing — which is why Ways 1 and 2 are worth having.

Open line, : divide top and bottom by first, then let :

Intuition — why they are purely imaginary

A lossless line with a lossless termination cannot dissipate anything. Whatever goes in comes back out. So the input impedance must be a pure reactance — a component that stores energy and gives it back. The line has become a capacitor or an inductor, depending only on its length.

This is the central microwave trick: at GHz frequencies you build inductors and capacitors out of lengths of copper, not out of components.

The length map — memorise this table

→ capacitive → inductive

Intuition — why a short "becomes" an open at

Two ways to see it, both worth knowing:

Rotation: a short is , sitting on the far left of the -circle. Rotate (a move) and you land on : an open.

Standing wave: a short forces at the end — a voltage node. Nodes and antinodes alternate every . So a quarter wavelength back you are at a voltage antinode, which by the same argument is a current node. Voltage maximum with zero current means : an open. ✓

Practical payoff (your notes' last diagram): put a shorted stub across a line and it presents an open circuit — the signal is untouched. But at DC it is a dead short. So it is a mechanical support and a DC ground path that is invisible to the RF signal. Antenna masts genuinely work this way.

Frequency dependence — a trap

"" is only at one frequency. A fixed physical length has , which grows with frequency. Your notes' plot of versus frequency at fixed makes this point: the shorted stub is inductive, then resonant (open) at , then capacitive, then a short again at , and so on periodically. Every stub-based trick is inherently narrowband.

How to read that plot

The stub never changes. The frequency does. One fixed piece of shorted copper walks through every reactance there is, simply because grows with — the same length is a different number of wavelengths at every frequency.

The zeros and the poles alternate every quarter wave. Zeros of (the stub looks like a short) sit where is a multiple of ; poles (it looks like an open) sit where is an odd multiple of . Between them the sign of tells you which component you have built.

Read the DC end. At , , so your stub is zero wavelengths long and : a dead short, exactly as a piece of wire to ground should be. That corner of the graph is what makes the antenna-mast trick work.

Read the steepness. Near the curve is almost vertical — a 10% change in frequency swings the reactance from a few hundred ohms inductive, through infinity, to a few hundred ohms capacitive. That vertical stretch is the narrowband limitation, drawn. For , m/s and cm (so GHz):

behaves as
DCshort
0.8 GHzinductor
0.9 GHzinductor
1.0 GHzopen
1.1 GHzcapacitor
1.2 GHzcapacitor

Move just 10% off the design frequency and a perfect open has become a 316 Ω reactance — and the sign has flipped on the way through. Every stub trick in this course inherits that fragility, which is the honest answer to "what are the limitations of your design?"

Exam

Intuition

Delivered power = incident power − reflected power. Nothing more mysterious than that. The forward wave carries toward the load; a fraction of it bounces straight back.

Notice , not — power goes as amplitude squared. A "modest" reflects only 9% of the power. This is why VSWR 2 (, 11% reflected) is often considered acceptable.

Also: since is constant along a lossless line, is the same at every point. Energy is not accumulating anywhere. That is a good consistency check.

Exam

SECTION 14Lossy transmission lines

Real conductors have resistance, and real dielectrics leak. Add two more per-unit-length elements:

  • (Ω/m) in series — ohmic loss in the conductors.
  • (S/m) in shunt — leakage through the insulator.
First — where and actually come from

They are not the same kind of thing, and knowing which is which tells you what to expect.

is the copper. Current flowing along the conductors meets their finite conductivity and heats them. At high frequency the current is squeezed into a thin skin at the conductor surface (the skin effect), so the useful cross-section shrinks as frequency rises and grows roughly as . It is not a constant.

is the insulator. The dielectric between the conductors is not perfect: a small current leaks straight across, and the dielectric also absorbs energy as its molecules are repeatedly polarised. Both effects are bundled into , and because the polarisation loss is proportional to how often you flip the field, grows roughly as .

So and are frequency-dependent, whereas and are fixed by the geometry. This is why a cable's datasheet quotes attenuation as a curve against frequency, not a single number — and why nothing in this section may be assumed constant across a wide band.

is not a resistor you could measure with a multimeter. At DC a good coax has essentially infinite insulation resistance. Almost all of is polarisation loss, which only exists when the field is changing. Setting at low frequency is usually a good approximation; at microwave it is not.

Derivation — the general line

Step 1 — the circuit equations. The slice model of Section 1 gains two elements: a resistance in series with the inductor, and a conductance in parallel with the capacitor. KVL now includes the resistor's drop, and KCL includes the leakage current:

Read them as before: voltage now falls along the line for two reasons — the inductor fighting a changing current, and the resistor simply dropping volts. Current falls for two reasons — charging the capacitor, and leaking across the conductance.

Step 2 — phasors. In sinusoidal steady state , and both equations become ordinary derivatives in alone:

The one substitution that makes this whole section easy

which is exactly the pair you already solved in Section 7 — only the two coefficients have changed. So the answers must have exactly the same shape, and in fact everything in this course reduces to two formulas:

Memorise these two and you never need to memorise anything else in Sections 3 or 14. Set (so , ) and they hand back the lossless results immediately:

Note the pleasing symmetry: is the product under the root, the ratio. Propagation cares about how much impedance and admittance the wave meets; impedance cares about their balance.

Step 3 — decouple. Same manoeuvre as Sections 2 and 7. Differentiate the first equation with respect to , then substitute the second:

Define and the equation takes its final form:

Watch the sign — it is not the same equation as before

The lossless version was , with a minus. This one is , with a plus. Nothing has gone wrong: in the lossless limit, so and the two agree. But it does mean you must not carry the old minus sign across, and it is why the solutions are written here and there. Same solutions, different packaging.

Step 4 — solve. "Differentiate twice, get back a positive multiple of yourself" is solved by real exponentials in :

Split into its real and imaginary parts and the forward wave separates into two factors that do two different jobs:

has magnitude 1 and only turns the phasor — that is propagation, exactly as before. is real and less than 1 — that is the new part, the amplitude bleeding away. The wave still travels at ; it just arrives smaller.

Step 5 — characteristic impedance. Put the forward wave alone into . The left side differentiates to , and the right side is , so

What changes physically when goes complex

On a lossless line is real, so in a single travelling wave the voltage and current are exactly in phase — they peak together, everywhere.

Once is complex, a single forward wave has its current lagging (or leading) its voltage by . That phase angle is the loss: no longer accounts for all the energy passing a point, and the shortfall is what the line absorbs between here and there.

It also breaks a convenience you have been leaning on. "Matched" now means with complex — a plain resistor can no longer perfectly terminate a lossy line. In practice is a fraction of a degree for any decent cable, which is exactly why 50 Ω resistors work.

A real does not prove the line is lossless

Everyone learns "lossless real" and then silently runs the implication backwards. It does not hold. Take the opposite extreme of a good line — the very lossy case, and , which is what an ordinary telegraph cable looks like at low frequency. Then the terms are the negligible ones:

is perfectly real, and yet the line is nothing but loss — is real, meaning pure attenuation with almost no phase shift. The signal does not propagate so much as diffuse. Shevgaonkar states this explicitly (§2.14): a nearly-real tells you the line is at one extreme or the other, and you need to say which.

The real cost of loss is not attenuation — it is dispersion

Attenuation is annoying but curable: put an amplifier in. The deeper problem is that is, in general, not proportional to .

Phase velocity is . If the cancels and every frequency travels at the same speed, so a pulse holds its shape. If it does not, each Fourier component of your pulse moves at a different speed, they drift out of step, and the pulse spreads until it overlaps its neighbours. No amplifier fixes that — amplifying a smeared pulse gives a louder smeared pulse.

This was the actual engineering crisis of the first transatlantic telegraph cables, and it is the reason this whole theory exists. Two escapes from it appear in this course: work where and (the low-loss approximation below, where is linear again), or satisfy the Heaviside condition of the next box, which makes exactly linear no matter how lossy the line is.

The distortionless line — Heaviside's condition

This is not in the body of the textbook chapter, but it is set as Problems 2.3 and 2.36, so it is fair game. The question: can a line be lossy and still not distort?

Yes. Suppose the primary constants happen to satisfy

Then and share the identical bracket, so it comes straight out of the square root:

Look at what that gives you:

  • is exactly linear in , so for every frequency. No dispersion at all.
  • is independent of frequency, so every component is attenuated by the same factor. The pulse comes out smaller but perfectly shaped.
  • is real and frequency-independent, exactly as in the lossless case.

The engineering punchline. Real cables have — far too much series resistance for their leakage. You cannot easily reduce . But you can deliberately increase until the ratios match, by inserting lumped inductors at intervals along the line. This is called loading, and it is what rescued long-distance telephony. Note the trade: loading raises , which lowers and raises , and you accept that to buy an undistorted pulse.

Choosing the square root

has two square roots, . Always pick the one with , so that decays as the forward wave moves in . A growing wave in a passive medium would be unphysical. Your notes flag this explicitly.

Names

  • — attenuation constant, nepers/m. Amplitude falls as . (1 neper = 8.686 dB.)
  • — phase constant, rad/m. Same role as before.

The low-loss approximation (, )

Derivation — binomial expansion

Both small quantities, so use :

Matching real and imaginary parts:

(The second form uses and .)

And — unchanged, still real. Convenient.

Intuition

To first order, loss does not change how fast the wave goes or what impedance the line presents — it just makes the wave fade. splits cleanly into a conductor part () and a dielectric part (), so you can attribute attenuation to its physical cause.

Note also that is linear in , meaning all frequencies travel at the same speed — no dispersion, so pulse shapes survive. When the low-loss condition fails (as on long telegraph cables at low frequency) stops being linear, different frequencies travel at different speeds, and pulses smear into each other. That was the actual engineering crisis that produced this theory.

SECTION 15Lossy resonators and the Q factor

A shorted lossy line near behaves as a resonant circuit. This is how microwave resonators are built.

Start here — what a "resonator" even means

You have already built one, in Section 12

Take the shorted stub you just met. At its design frequency it looks like an open circuit. Now look at what it does as you sweep frequency — that is exactly the plot in Section 12:

  • at DC it is a dead short ();
  • as rises it becomes inductive (, growing);
  • at it blows up to an open ();
  • just above that it flips to capacitive;
  • and at it is a short again.

Now compare that with a component you already know: a parallel LC tank. Inductive below resonance, infinite at resonance, capacitive above it. Identical behaviour.

That is the whole idea of this section. A shorted stub is a parallel resonant circuit. Not "behaves a bit like one" — near you can replace it with an , and in parallel and no measurement at the terminals could tell the difference.

Why the word "resonance" is the right word

Resonance always means the same thing: energy sloshing back and forth between two stores, with almost nothing lost per cycle. A pendulum trades height for speed. An LC tank trades electric field in for magnetic field in .

The stub does exactly this. Section 8 showed that on a fully reflecting line no power reaches the far end — instead energy piles into the electric field at voltage antinodes, then a quarter cycle later into the magnetic field at current antinodes, and back again, forever. A totally reflecting line is not a transmission system, it is a resonator. This section takes that seriously and asks how good a one it is.

The string analogy — and the exact string to picture

Everything here is genuinely the same physics as a vibrating string: same wave equation, same reflections, same standing waves. But the analogy only clicks if you pick the right string, and the obvious one is wrong.

Not a guitar string. That is clamped at both ends, so both ends are nodes and the fundamental is long. That is the model for a line shorted at both ends.

The right picture is a string fixed at one end and free at the other — tied to a wall at one end, threaded through a frictionless ring at the other. Fixed end = node, free end = antinode, and the fundamental is exactly long, with overtones at , … precisely the odd multiples this section keeps insisting on. In acoustics it is a stopped organ pipe or a clarinet: closed at one end, open at the other, sounding a quarter-wave fundamental.

StringTransmission line
displacement voltage
tied to a wall — forced, pulse flips overshort circuit, , voltage node
free end on a frictionless ring — swings widestopen circuit, , voltage antinode
mass per length, tension and per unit length
damping — how fast it dies, and hence

So where is the "open" on a shorted stub? This is the bit worth getting straight. The far end is physically shorted — that is the wall. The input end, where you connect to your circuit, is the free end: a voltage antinode, swinging widest. And an antinode is exactly maximum voltage with zero current, which is what means.

So "the stub presents an open circuit" and "the input end is a voltage antinode" are the same sentence. If you were thinking that an antinode should sit at the driven end — you were right, and that antinode is the open circuit.

Plucking versus bowing — and why both measure

Careful to separate two different things: where the boundaries are (fixed or free) and how you excite it.

Plucking is a one-off kick. Displace the string, let go, and it rings down at its natural frequencies. That is the transient picture — Sections 4–6, a step launched onto the line, echoes rattling back and forth and decaying. How many swings before it dies is the time reading of .

Bowing or blowing drives the system continuously at one frequency. That is the sinusoidal steady state — Sections 7 onward, a generator holding the line at one . Sweep the driving frequency and the response peaks sharply at resonance; how narrow that peak is is the frequency reading of .

Same resonator, same , two experiments. This is the church bell from the box above: it rings for a long time and has a definite pitch, and those are one fact seen from two sides.

A real detail the analogy even gets right: where you pluck a string decides which harmonics you excite (pluck at the midpoint and you get no even harmonics, because you are forcing an antinode where they need a node). The same is true of a stub — where you tap into it decides which of the modes you couple to.

So where exactly are you "bowing"?

At the input end — the junction, a quarter wavelength away from the short. The shorted end is the wall: you build it and never touch it again. Everything you connect, measure or drive happens at the other end.

But you are not obliged to tap right at the very end, and this is where the analogy earns its keep. You can connect anywhere along the stub, and the impedance you meet depends on where, exactly as Section 12 says — with measured from the short:

Tap at (for )What is happening there
(the short)Voltage node, current maximum
Conveniently matches a 50 Ω system
Climbing fast
(the input)Voltage antinode, current zero

So "where do I drive it?" is really the question "how hard do I want to couple?", and you answer it by choosing the tap point.

Why you must not drive hard at the antinode — loaded

Here is the trap. is the unloaded : the resonator sitting alone, losing energy only to its own . The moment you attach a source or a load you add another loss path, in parallel with the resonator's own :

Take the running example: , Np/m, , giving and . Now connect things to it:

What you attach at the antinodeLoaded
nothing50
100 kΩ (very weak tap)48.5
10 kΩ (weak tap)37.9
50 Ω source, connected directly0.77

Bolting a 50 Ω source straight onto a 3183 Ω resonator drops the from 50 to below 1 — it is not a resonator any more, it is a resistor. You destroyed the thing you were trying to use.

The fix is exactly the tap table above: connect at , where the stub already looks like 50 Ω, or couple weakly through a small capacitor or a small loop. Deliberately choosing the coupling so that is what you want — high for a narrow filter, lower for a usable bandwidth — is most of resonator design.

Two ways in, and the standing wave tells you which to use

There are two places on the stub where coupling is easy, and they are opposite ends with opposite methods.

At the open input end: voltage is maximum, current is zero. Couple electrically — a probe, or a small series capacitor. You are grabbing the electric field.

At the shorted end: voltage is zero, current is maximum. You cannot excite it with a voltage there — it is a node — but you can with a current loop, grabbing the magnetic field.

This is not a curiosity; it is how real microwave cavities are fed. Look inside one and you will find either a little probe antenna poking into a voltage maximum, or a small wire loop sitting in a current maximum. The standing-wave picture tells you where to put which.

The string does the same thing: you cannot get a fixed-free string going by pushing sideways at the wall, but you can by shaking the free end — or, more weakly, by nudging it somewhere in between, which is exactly a tap at intermediate .

What means, before any formula

Three ways to say the same thing

is one number answering "how good is this resonator?", and it has three equivalent readings. Get comfortable with all three, because exams use whichever is convenient.

ReadingQuestion it answersHigh means
EnergyHow much is stored, compared with how much leaks away each cycle?Loses very little per swing
TimeHow many oscillations before it dies out?Rings for a long time
FrequencyHow narrow is the peak?Very selective filter

The everyday version: strike a church bell and it rings for ten seconds — high . Strike a cardboard box and you get a dull thud — low . The bell also has a very definite pitch while the thud does not, and that is the frequency reading of the same fact. Ringing for a long time and having a sharp pitch are not two properties; they are one property seen in two domains.

The formal definition is the energy one, and it is the one everything is derived from:

Why loss cannot be ignored here — the one place in this course

Everywhere else, setting is a harmless simplification. Here it destroys the problem. Lossless theory says the peak in that plot is infinitely tall and infinitely narrow: , , bandwidth .

That is not a resonator you can use. You could not couple power into it, you could not build a filter with it, and it would never dissipate anything. The entire content of this section is the small quantity . Carry it, even though you have been dropping it for the last ten sections.

Look at resonance. The derivation above gives , a positive real resistance — which is exactly right, because at resonance a parallel looks resistive, and the line really is burning power. Multiply by and you get a pure reactance, i.e. a lossy line that dissipates nothing. Also a contradiction.

What that number is actually for

It is easy to read as just "some big number" and move on. It is the single most useful quantity in the section, for three reasons.

1. It is the of the equivalent tank. Near resonance the stub is a parallel , and this is its resistance. Once you have you can go back to ordinary circuit theory — how much a load will damp it, where to tap it, how to couple in.

2. It tells you the impedance level to design around. With , Np/m and :

A 50 Ω cable behaving as a 3.2 kΩ resistor. If you tried to drive that from a 50 Ω source without thinking, you would swamp the resonator completely.

3. It gives you , and therefore bandwidth. The derivation below needs , and this is the it uses. Substituting and collapses it to a memorable form:

So the resonator's resistance is about times the line impedance — the transmission-line version of the standard tank result . High and high resonant resistance are the same statement. (Check: ✓)

Note what does and does not depend on length: does, but does not. A longer resonator has a lower resonant resistance but stores proportionally more energy, so its is unchanged.

Step 2 — the standing wave that stores the energy

To use you need two things: the stored energy , and the power lost . Both come from the same picture — the standing wave sitting on the resonant section.

Reading the energy off that picture

Energy density in the electric field is per unit length; in the magnetic field . Since and vary along the line, you have to integrate rather than just multiply — that is the only reason an integral appears.

The useful trick: at the instant the voltage peaks everywhere, the current is zero everywhere, so all the energy is electric at that moment. Integrate the electric part alone and you have the total. A quarter cycle later it is all magnetic, and the total is the same number. You never need to add them — and adding them is exactly the mistake in the box further down.

Two factors of 2 that cancel — do not copy the shortcut

Your lecture notes write and . Both are exactly twice the values derived above. The energy line adds the peak electric energy and the peak magnetic energy as though they happened at the same moment — they are a quarter cycle apart, so only one of them is present at a time. The power line uses where the cycle-average is .

The two errors sit in the same ratio, so still comes out right. But that is luck, not method: reproduce one of them in an exam and pair it with the correct form of the other and your is wrong by a factor of 2. Use the four steps above, or quote directly and skip the energy bookkeeping entirely.

Equivalently, since : — a high- resonator is one where the wave can travel many wavelengths before being absorbed. It rings for a long time.

Notice what is not in the answer: length. depends only on the line's material quality, not how long you cut it. Making a resonator longer adds stored energy and loss in equal measure.

SECTION 16Quarter-wave impedance matching

The payoff. You have a source designed for (say 50 Ω) and a load that is not 50 Ω. Reflections waste power. Fix it with a single length of the right cable.

Intuition — why the geometric mean

The line inverts normalised impedance. Normalised to its own , the load looks like ; after inversion it looks like ; de-normalising gives . Setting that equal to says the transformer must sit exactly "halfway" between and — but multiplicatively, i.e. the geometric mean, because impedance transformation here is a multiplication, not an addition.

Analogy: it is the optical anti-reflection coating. To stop light reflecting between glass () and air () you coat with a quarter-wavelength layer of index . Identical mathematics, identical reason.

Two limitations you should state in an answer
  1. Narrowband. The section is only at the design frequency. Move off it and , the transformation is wrong, and reflections return. (Broadband versions use several cascaded sections.)
  2. Real loads only. needs real, or comes out complex, which no passive line can have. For a complex your notes give the standard fix: move back along the line to a point where the impedance is real (there is one every — at each voltage maximum and each minimum), and put the transformer there.

Where this goes next

Section 16 is where Part I stops, but the story does not. Three loose ends are tied up in Part II:

  • The transformer needs a cable of a specific , and B9 shows depends only logarithmically on geometry — so the value you want is often simply not manufacturable. The practical answer is stub matching (B6), which uses only the line you already have.
  • For a complex load this section told you to "move back to a point where the impedance is real". B1 shows you where those points are on the Smith chart (the two crossings of the real axis) and B6 does the whole design graphically.

SECTION 19Traps, sign conventions and sanity checks

The eight ways to lose marks
  1. The origin of moves half way through the course. Sections 4–6 (transients) put the generator at and the load at , so is a wave running in away from the source. Sections 7 onwards (phasors) put the load at and the generator at , which is what makes evaluate cleanly and come out with a minus sign.

    Your lecture notes switch in exactly the same place, so this is not an error in either — but it is the single most effective way to produce a sign mistake, because both halves use the letter for different things. Before writing anything down, decide which picture you are in and mark the origin on your diagram. If a formula from Section 5 and one from Section 11 appear in the same line of algebra, one of them needs its sign flipped.

  2. Direction of . is measured from the load, backwards toward the generator. Getting this backwards flips the sign in and rotates you the wrong way.
  3. The minus sign in . . Nearly every derivation depends on it.

  5. and are per unit length. Units H/m and F/m. Multiply by before using them as lumped values (e.g. in the derivation).
  6. Choosing the branch of . When solving something, there are infinitely many roots. Use the physics (inductive vs capacitive, shortest length) to pick.
  7. for power, for voltage.
  8. . Always pick the decaying root of .
Sanity checks to run on any answer
  • Is ? If not, you have made an algebra error (or the load is active).
  • Is VSWR ? Always.
  • For a lossless line with a lossless termination (open/short/pure reactance), is purely imaginary? It must be.
  • Does the transient answer converge to the DC voltage divider ?
  • Does return to when ? Good check on your .
  • Does the matched case () give , VSWR , for all ? Every general formula must collapse to this.
One mental model to carry into the exam

Everything in this course is one story told four ways:

Time domain: a pulse travels, hits a mismatch, part bounces back.
Frequency domain: forward and backward phasors interfere into a standing wave.
Impedance: the line transforms into as you walk away from it.
Geometry: rotates clockwise on a circle of fixed radius, one full turn per .

They are the same fact. If a question feels hard in one language, translate it into another. Most "hard" transmission-line problems are easy in the -circle picture.

SECTION B1The Smith chart, properly

Section 10 told you the -plane is "the Smith chart before the grid is printed on it". Here is the grid, where it comes from, and how to actually use it.

Why a chart at all

Every line calculation is the same two-step dance: convert between and , and rotate . Rotation is trivial in the -plane and horrible in the -plane; conversion is the other way round. The Smith chart's whole idea is to draw the -plane grid on top of the -plane disc, so you can rotate geometrically and read impedance directly. It replaces a page of complex arithmetic with a protractor and a compass.

The five landmarks

Line AB (the horizontal diameter) is every purely resistive load. The outer circle is every purely reactive load. Upper half inductive, lower half capacitive.

Constant-VSWR circles, and the rule that matters

From Section 10, moving along a lossless line keeps fixed and only turns its phase. On the chart that is a circle centred on M, of radius . So:

The single most useful sentence about the Smith chart

Moving along the line = rotating about the centre. Nothing else moves. Towards the generator is clockwise; towards the load is anticlockwise. One full turn is , i.e. — which is why everything repeats every half wavelength.

And: the closer your point is to the centre, the better the match. M itself is ; the rim is .

The single most common Smith chart mistake

You rotate by , not . The factor of two is the round trip — the wave goes to the load and comes back, so the reflected wave picks up the phase twice.

This is not a hypothetical error. Shevgaonkar's own Example 2.21 makes it: with cm and a voltage minimum cm from the load, , and the book rotates the chart by instead of . Its printed answer is wrong; the correct load is

You can catch the error without redoing anything, using the book's own rule (B3 below): the voltage maximum was nearer the load, which means the load must be inductive. The book's answer is capacitive. If a Smith chart answer contradicts the standing-wave pattern that produced it, you have rotated by the wrong amount.

The chart rim is graduated in rather than degrees precisely so you never have to compute by hand: half a turn is marked , a full turn . The factor of two is baked into the scale.

SECTION B2The admittance chart

Stubs go in parallel with the line, and parallel elements add admittances, not impedances. So all matching work is done in admittance. Happily, no new chart is needed.

Derivation — why the same chart works upside down

Normalised admittance is . Substitute into the definition of :

Compare the two ends. The formula in is identical to the formula in apart from an overall minus sign — and multiplying a complex number by is a rotation of .

The consequence — two facts, one operation

1. The admittance chart is the impedance chart rotated . Read the same printed grid with and , remembering the axes now point the other way.

2. To convert , take the point diagonally opposite through the centre — same VSWR circle, half a turn round.

And here is the elegant part. Half a turn is a move along the line. So "invert the impedance" and "walk a quarter wavelength" are literally the same operation on this chart — which is Section 11's , now obvious rather than algebraic.

Three traps when you switch charts
  • The upper half changes meaning. is inductive, but is capacitive (since ). Same half of the same chart, opposite component.
  • Short and open swap. Point A is a short in impedance, an open in admittance; B is the reverse.
  • Maxima and minima swap. The right-hand real axis point is a voltage maximum read as impedance, and a voltage minimum (current maximum) read as admittance.

The book's one-line summary is worth memorising: voltage standing-wave pattern is to impedance as current standing-wave pattern is to admittance.

SECTION B3Measuring an unknown load: the slotted line

Section 18 Type 5 gave you the recipe. Here is the instrument, the closed-form answer, and the trick that makes it work in practice. This is Shevgaonkar §2.12.1 and §2.15, and it is heavily examined.

Why you cannot just use a voltmeter

At microwave frequencies you cannot measure phase reliably — the probe leads are themselves a significant fraction of a wavelength. But you can measure amplitude, and you can measure position with a ruler. A slotted line is a rigid line with a narrow longitudinal slot, along which a diode probe slides, reading . Everything below extracts a complex from amplitude-and-position data only.

What three readings give you
  1. Spacing between adjacent minima . This hands you and hence — measured, not assumed. You never need to know or .
  2. . This gives — the magnitude.
  3. Distance of a minimum from the load. This gives — the phase.

Magnitude plus phase is the whole complex , hence the whole complex . Two rulers and a diode.

Derivation — the closed form

At a voltage minimum the impedance is real and minimal (Section 11): . Treat that as a known load sitting a distance in front of the real load, and transform backwards — i.e. use form (B) with length , writing :

Multiply top and bottom by :

Separating real and imaginary parts:

Sanity: gives , . ✓ And carries the factor , so its sign is set purely by .

Read the load off the pattern before you calculate

This costs nothing and catches sign errors instantly. Walking from the load outwards:

Standing-wave patternLoad
A maximum lies nearer the loadInductive
A minimum lies nearer the loadCapacitive
Max or min sits exactly at the loadPurely resistive (max , min )

Review Question 2.41 is exactly this, in five parts.

Two practical points that get asked

Why minima rather than maxima? A minimum is sharp and a maximum is flat, so a minimum's position can be located far more precisely. Near a null, a small movement produces a large fractional change in reading; near a peak, almost none.

Where is the load plane? This is the real difficulty. A connector has physical extent and you cannot point at the exact plane . The fix: replace the load with a good short and re-record the pattern. A short forces a null exactly at the load plane, so the nulls of the shorted pattern mark planes electrically identical to the load plane. Measure from one of those, and the connector's own length cancels out.

Both minima adjacent to a reference plane work, since ; use whichever with the correct sign.

A bonus method: VSWR from the width of the null

If is large, is tiny and the ratio is swamped by detector noise. Instead measure the width of the minimum at the level :

All the information now comes from two position readings, which are precise, instead of an amplitude ratio, which is not. For a sharp null , so — the narrower the null, the higher the VSWR. This is Problem 2.49.
