SECTION B5Power, and what "matched" really means

Real power is the same everywhere; reactive power is not

Section 13 showed is independent of position. That is only half the story. Taking the full complex power at distance :

The real part has no in it. The imaginary part does — it rotates with like everything else.

The physical reading: energy flow is uniform along a lossless line (it must be — nothing absorbs energy in between), but energy storage is not. Standing waves pile electric energy at voltage antinodes and magnetic energy at current antinodes, and the local imbalance between the two is what the reactive power measures. Review Question 2.34 asks exactly this, and "because the line is lossless" only answers the first half.

Two different meanings of "matched" — do not conflate them
Load matchConjugate (generator) match
Condition
AchievesNo reflection; , Maximum power delivered
Depends on , ?NoYes — depends on both

These are genuinely different goals and they usually disagree. Maximum power transfer is the lumped-circuit criterion , applied at the generator terminals where the "load" is . Since swings all around a circle as and change, a conjugate match holds only at one length and one frequency.

The exception, and the reason for the whole matching industry: if and , then for every length and every frequency at once. Both criteria are satisfied simultaneously and permanently. That is why equipment is built to a standard impedance rather than tuned per installation.

Two traps in power questions

Peak or RMS? has the only for peak-amplitude phasors. If the question quotes RMS values, drop it. The book flags this in Example 2.15 and it is a standard way to lose marks.

Percentage delivered. . Note this is the fraction of incident power, not of available generator power — those coincide only when .

SECTION B6Stub matching: single and double

Section 16's quarter-wave transformer has a crippling practical flaw: every different load needs a different , i.e. a physically different cable. Stub matching fixes that by using only the line you already have. This is Shevgaonkar §2.13.2–3, and it is the most heavily examined design topic in the chapter.

The idea, in one paragraph

Walking along the line changes both the real and imaginary parts of the admittance at once, so you cannot "steer" to by walking alone. But you get one free move: walk until the real part is right, then kill the imaginary part with a component. And the component is free too, because Section 12 showed a length of shorted line is a pure reactance. Two lengths of the same cable, and any load is matched.

Why admittance, and why shunt

The stub is connected across the line — in parallel. Parallel elements add admittances. So the entire procedure is done on the admittance chart, and "adding a stub" means "adding to the current point", which is a slide along a constant- circle. Working in impedance here would force you to compute a parallel combination at every step.

Single-stub matching

Procedure — the two unknowns are (where) and (how long)
  1. Normalise the load, , and mark it. Draw the constant-VSWR circle through it.
  2. Take the diagonally opposite point — that is (Section B2). From here on read the chart as admittance.
  3. Rotate clockwise (towards the generator) until you hit the circle. The VSWR circle always cuts it, at two points and . The arc travelled is , the stub location.
  4. At the admittance is . The real part is already right; you need to cancel .
  5. So the stub must supply susceptance . Mark on the outer () circle and measure the arc anticlockwise to the short-circuit point. That arc is the stub length .

Then : matched, and everything to the left of the junction sees .

Why there are always exactly two answers

A circle centred on the origin cuts the circle in two places, and , symmetric about the real axis. At the admittance is and the stub supplies ; at it is and the stub supplies , with length . Both are valid matches. Choose on practical grounds — usually whichever gives the shorter stub or the more convenient junction position.

And a shorted stub can always be swapped for an open one of length different. On microstrip an open stub is easier (a short needs a via drilled through the substrate); on coax a short is easier (an open end radiates). This choice is engineering, not physics, and saying so earns marks.

The drawback that motivates the double stub

For a fixed load, a single stub is excellent. For a varying load it is useless: both and must change, and is the position of a physical junction. Moving it means unsoldering the stub, or drilling a new hole in the outer conductor of a coax. Not something you do while tuning.

Double-stub matching

Fix the stub positions permanently and adjust only the two lengths — two things you can trim with a sliding short. The standard spacing between the stubs is .

Procedure

Label the junctions (first stub, nearer the load) and (second stub). For a match at we need , so just before the second stub must be — on the circle.

Working backwards from to means rotating anticlockwise by . So the target set at is the circle rotated anticlockwise about the centre. Draw that auxiliary circle first; it is the whole trick.

  1. Mark ; rotate clockwise by to reach .
  2. The first stub can only change susceptance, so from you may slide along the constant- circle. Slide until you meet the rotated circle, at .
  3. First stub must supply . Convert that to a length as before.
  4. Rotate clockwise by along its own VSWR circle. By construction you land on the circle, at .
  5. Second stub supplies . Convert to a length. Done.
The forbidden region — the standard exam question

Constant- circles are nested. If lands on a constant- circle that lies entirely inside the rotated circle, step 2 can never reach the target and no match exists. The boundary is the constant- circle externally tangent to the rotated circle.

Two points that are usually the marks:

  • The constraint is on , the conductance after travelling — not on the load itself. So changing can always rescue a "forbidden" load. Nothing is permanently unmatchable.
  • The fix that needs no relocation is a triple-stub tuner: three stubs at spacing, use whichever adjacent pair works, and disable the unused one by setting it to — a shorted stub looks like an open circuit at the junction and is therefore invisible. This matches everything without moving anything.
"Why ?"

A genuine question with a genuine answer, and it is asked. Smaller spacing rotates the auxiliary circle further left, enlarging the forbidden region — worst at . Larger spacing pushes the working area into the crowded right-hand region of the chart where the grid lines bunch up, so a small graphical slip becomes a large impedance error. is the compromise; behaves identically by symmetry.

A counter-intuitive fact worth knowing (§2.13.4)

After matching, the line back to the generator is flat, . Between the matching unit and the load, however, the standing wave is larger than it was before you matched anything:

Always. The reason is simple once stated: after matching, the generator sees and therefore delivers its full power no matter what the load is. A stubbornly reactive load can only absorb that power by developing a very large voltage and current. In the limit of a purely reactive load the standing-wave amplitude diverges.

So matching does not remove the standing wave — it confines it to the short section beyond the tuner, where you can afford it. Practical consequence: the voltage rating of that last stretch of cable, and of the tuner itself, is what limits your power handling.

SECTION B7Resonators: series, parallel, bandwidth and voltage step-up

Section 15 derived for one case. The book treats the resonator as a component in its own right, and three things it adds are examinable.

1. Which resonance you get

A lossless stub is either a short or an open at every multiple of (Section 12). With loss included, "open" becomes a large real impedance and "short" a small one — which is exactly what parallel and series resonance mean.

The pattern is worth a sentence rather than memorisation: a shorted stub starts at a short (series-like) and alternates every ; an open stub does the opposite. Both come from the same two formulas,

evaluated where or .

The one place you may not neglect loss

Everywhere else in this course is a fine approximation. Here it is fatal: set and the parallel-resonant impedance is infinite, is infinite, and the bandwidth is zero. The entire content of a resonator calculation is the small quantity . Carry it.

2. Bandwidth

The result that makes useful

This is what is for. "High " means "sharply selective" — a filter that passes a narrow band and rejects everything else. Section 15's "rings for a long time" and this "narrow bandwidth" are the same statement in the two domains, linked by the Fourier uncertainty relation.

Worked example (the book's Example 2.23) — do this one

A 75 Ω line with attenuation 1.5 dB/m is used as a resonator at 1 GHz, with m/s. Find , the bandwidth, and for a 5 cm series-resonant section.

Convert dB to nepers first — exponentials only ever take nepers:

Note the shape of the answer: an 11 MHz window out of 1 GHz — about 1% — from an ordinary piece of cable. That selectivity is unreachable with lumped and at these frequencies, and it is why microwave filters are made of metalwork.

3. The line as a voltage step-up transformer

Why a piece of cable can multiply voltage by 100

Take a section shorted at one end () and open at the other (). Follow one round trip: the wave picks up of phase from travelling there-and-back, plus another from the reflection at the short (the open contributes nothing, ). Total — it returns exactly in phase with itself.

So each round trip adds constructively to what is already there. The amplitude climbs until the loss per round trip balances the input, and the only thing stopping it is :

A of a few hundred therefore buys a voltage step-up of a few hundred, with no transformer, no core and no windings — just resonant build-up. It is the same physics as pushing a swing in time with its own period.

The catch, which is the exam point: that ratio holds at no load. Draw any real current at and you add loss, which drops , which drops the step-up. The high voltage exists precisely because nothing is using it.

SECTION B8Lossy lines: when the circle becomes a spiral

Section 14 gave and for a lossy line but kept using the lossless picture of reflections. Two things genuinely change.

VSWR is no longer a single number

With loss, picks up a decaying magnitude as well as a rotating phase. Measuring from the load towards the generator:

The factor of 2 is the round trip, as always — the reflected wave has travelled the distance twice, so it is attenuated twice. Feeding this into the definition of VSWR:

now depends on where you measure it, falling steadily towards 1 as you move away from the load. Consequences: the ripple visibly dies out as you walk towards the generator, and successive maxima are not exactly apart, because the decaying envelope pulls each extremum slightly off the lossless position.

The trap: a long lossy line looks perfectly matched

If then and the generator sees . Every instrument reports a beautiful match — , no reflected power.

But nothing has been matched. The power is not reaching the load; it is being burnt in the cable. A reflection does come back from the mismatched load, it is simply too attenuated to return.

So a good VSWR reading does not prove power is reaching the antenna. This is a real and expensive failure mode in the field, and it is also occasionally exploited deliberately: a lossy line makes a crude isolator, protecting a source from reflections at the cost of throwing away signal.

On the Smith chart: a spiral, not a circle

Constant was the whole basis of the circle. With loss, shrinks as you rotate, so the locus spirals inwards towards the matched centre.

The practical procedure: do the lossless construction, then correct radially.

  1. Mark and draw its VSWR circle.
  2. Rotate clockwise by as usual, reaching .
  3. Move radially inwards by , reaching .
  4. Read at .

Printed Smith charts carry a "transmission loss, 1 dB steps" scale along the bottom for exactly this correction. Within any one section the VSWR may be taken constant; it steps down from section to section.

Note which way it goes: loss always moves you towards the centre, i.e. towards an apparent match. That is the same trap as the box above, drawn as a picture.

SECTION B9Measuring the line itself, and real cables

Getting , and from two measurements

Section 12 gave . That is half of a complete characterisation method (§2.15): take an arbitrary length of the cable and measure its input impedance twice, once open-circuited and once shorted.

Derivation

Multiply them and the hyperbolics cancel; divide them and cancels:

is complex. Invert the using , remembering that a complex logarithm has infinitely many branches:

The ambiguity in is physical, not mathematical

is not a defect of the algebra. Input impedance repeats every , so the measurement genuinely cannot know how many half-wavelengths are buried inside . A 1 m cable and a 1 m cable with three extra half-waves in it present identical terminal impedances.

Fix 1 — use a short sample. If then by construction. The cost: is then tiny, so is the small difference of two similar numbers and comes out badly.

Fix 2 — the two-frequency method. Measure at , then raise the frequency slowly until and repeat. That happens at the where exactly one more half-wave has fitted into , so has advanced by precisely 1 — and you watched it happen rather than guessing:

Assumes and the loss are the same at both frequencies, which is fair over a small step.

Why measure at all, rather than compute ? Because the wave does not travel at . , so measuring measures the cable's actual velocity — the velocity factor , typically 0.66 for polyethylene coax. Getting this wrong makes every stub in your design the wrong length by a third.

Practical warning: a real "open" has fringing capacitance and a real "short" has loop inductance, so neither is ideal. Measure several lengths and extrapolate to cancel them.

Where comes from physically

is not something you choose — it falls out of the cross-sectional geometry. The three standard structures (§2.16):

LineTypical / standard
Coaxial
= inner diameter of outer conductor, = outer diameter of inner conductor		50 Ω (instruments), 75 Ω (video, TV)
Parallel wire
= centre-to-centre spacing, = wire diameter, valid for 		300 Ω ribbon, 600 Ω open line
Microstrip
= strip width, = substrate thickness; crude approximation		chosen to sit near 50 Ω
Reading the three formulas

They are all logarithmic in the geometry. To double on a coax you must square the diameter ratio. This is why the practical range of is so narrow — a few tens to a few hundred ohms — and why you cannot simply build a 5 Ω or 5000 Ω cable when a matching problem would like one. That constraint is precisely what makes stub matching (B6) more useful than the quarter-wave transformer.

Coax is inherently low impedance, parallel wire inherently high. Coax wraps the conductors closely round each other: large , small , so is small. Parallel wires held far apart do the opposite. The geometry is the impedance.

always divides. A denser dielectric raises , lowering both and together. You cannot change one without the other — hence the velocity factor above.

Why 50 Ω? For air coax, minimum attenuation occurs near 77 Ω and maximum power handling near 30 Ω. 50 Ω is roughly the compromise, and 75 Ω is the low-attenuation choice for receive-only work where power is irrelevant. Neither number is fundamental.

The microstrip expression is a crude approximation — real design uses the Hammerstad formulas or a solver — but note the 377 Ω: that is the intrinsic impedance of free space, showing up because a microstrip's field is half in the air.
